extracted.intended_audience: delegates to constitutional conventions, statesmen, and citizens concerned with framing government
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for structuring a republican constitution: how to divide powers, check ambitions, select representatives, organize the executive and judiciary, and avoid oligarchy or popular instability. Aimed at those framing or judging constitutions and laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three branches and separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Three branches of power have an unalterable foundation in nature; if all of them are not acknowledged in any constitution of government, it will be found to be imperfect, unstable, and soon enslaved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislative and executive authorities are naturally distinct; liberty and the laws depend entirely on a separation of them in the frame of government. This principle applies to every state in America and to the federal capacity. Examples and authorities are cited to show the necessity of three branches for balance and preservation of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative supremacy requires protections for the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative power is naturally and necessarily sovereign and supreme over the executive; therefore the latter must be made an essential branch of the former, even with a negative, or it will not be able to defend itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislature tends to dominate, the executive must possess institutional defenses (a negative/veto or other check) to avoid being invaded, undermined, or totally ruined by the legislative branch. Apply this to governors and other executives at state and federal levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for negatives (vetoes) in separate governments
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be found absolutely necessary to give negatives to the governors, to defend the executives against the influence of this [legislative] body, as well as the senates and representatives in their several states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessity of a negative in the house of representatives will be called in question by nobody. Negatives preserve the balance between branches and prevent legislative encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single assembly adequate for confederacies only with strong state checks
rubrics_metrics.description: A single assembly has been found to answer the purposes of confederacies very well, but deputies must be responsible to the states, their authority clearly ascertained, and the states in their separate capacities must be the checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deputies are accountable to their states and the states remain able to controul their delegates, a single council can work. The security against dangers of a single assembly depends on the accuracy and decision with which the governments of the separate states have their own orders arranged and balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully limit additional federal powers by comparative inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Before giving further federal powers (e.g., full power in foreign affairs, foreign commerce, or authority over interstate commerce), it is useful to compare ancient and modern leagues and confederacies with the circumstances, geography, commerce, population and forms of government to determine what federal powers are wanted and may be safely given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study historical examples (Greek confederacies, Swiss cantons, United Netherlands, Hanse towns) and compare to local conditions; the subject is delicate and requires caution and detailed enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent popular elections of at least one legislative branch
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular elections of one essential branch of the legislature, frequently repeated, are the only possible method of forming a free constitution, or of preserving the government of laws from the domination of men; when popular elections are given up, liberty and free government must be given up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a principal rule: keep at least one branch directly and frequently answerable to the people to prevent entrenchment and loss of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vesting executive power in an aristocratic senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting the nobility or senate into the management of the executive power deprives the representatives of the people of a voice in the legislature and tends to remove the eyes of the people from their representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume's plan (senate endowed with executive power) is criticized as a device to get rid of the people and their representatives; do not combine executive authority with an aristocratic body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection: small districts, frequent elections, local residency
rubrics_metrics.description: If county-members were abolished, and representatives proportionally and frequently chosen in small districts, and if no candidate could be chosen but an established long settled inhabitant of that district, it would be impossible to corrupt the people and the house might be an immortal guardian of national liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design electoral rules to make representatives truly local and accountable: small districts, frequent contests, residency qualifications to limit corruption and aristocratic influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive unity: prefer a single accountable executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power is properly the government; laws are a dead letter until an administration begins to carry them into execution. The unity, secrecy, and dispatch of one man has no equal; the executive power should be watched by all men and the attention of the whole nation fixed upon one point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vest executive authority in a single person to ensure prompt decision, secrecy where necessary, and a clear focus for accountability (impeachment, blame, censure). Avoid diffusing executive power among a large assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid full assembly appointment of officers — inefficiency & aristocratic capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Having an assembly of five hundred (or many) appoint generals, admirals, officers of revenue, police, justice, ambassadors, and other public officers exposes appointments to endless debate, delay, public exposure of candidates, and will result in selection by those with influence — generally aristocratic families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require the entire legislative assembly to appoint executive officers; such a procedure wastes time, creates opportunities for factional influence, and tends to favor the well-born and connected. Prefer executive appointment, lot, or smaller trusted bodies/committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice requires specialized tribunals and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly of five hundred men are totally incapable of administering justice: trial requires judges' knowledge of law, forms of proceeding, rules of evidence, confrontation of parties and witnesses, and often unanimity of juries to preserve rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial functions should be carried out by a specialized, independent judiciary with proper rules and procedures; do not submit criminal trials or judicial administration to the large legislative assembly or ad hoc committees chosen by faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large assemblies are ill-informed and inefficient for executive/judicial tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly must be informed before it can act. A large assembly of members collected from distant parts of a large state cannot become informed of merits and pretensions of candidates or of complex facts without consuming immense time; this causes confusion, uncertainty, and procrastination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve large assemblies for deliberative legislative functions where possible; rely on smaller bodies, committees, or executive officers for tasks requiring detailed information, secrecy, or dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent legislative entrenchment and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: If representatives begin to make distinctions and exceptions for themselves (franking letters, exemption from arrests, privilege of servants, exemption from taxes), their duration may extend from annual to life and they will form a system of subordination and dependence to themselves, governing all at their discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutionally forbid self-exemption, limit duration of terms, avoid cumulative privileges that lead to entrenchment; maintain frequent elections and limits to prevent assemblies turning into an oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple assemblies/bicameralism to divide functions and provide checks
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be two assemblies: one to divide, and the other to choose. Grant me this and confine both the convention and assembly to legislation, and give the whole executive power to another body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of roles across assemblies (e.g., one chamber for representation, another for review/selection) provides internal checks and prevents concentration of all governmental functions in a single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate long-term corruption with rotation and term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If long continuance of power may corrupt sincere men, the known expedient is that annually a third part of senators go out (i.e., rotation/staggered terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staggered terms and rotation in bodies that otherwise have long duration to reduce corruption risk while preserving continuity and experience.
